title: Windows toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6)
hookLine: Daniel keeps praying three times a day, windows open toward Jerusalem, lions or not
tomorrow: They that be wise shall shine (Daniel 12:3)

cards: The trap is a law. Under a new king, Darius, Daniel rises so high that the other officials go looking for something to accuse him of, and find nothing.
In the King James words: "We shall not find any occasion against this Daniel, except we find it against him concerning the law of his God." So they bring the king a flattering idea.

For thirty days, let no one ask a petition of any god or man except the king. Whoever does goes into the den of lions. The king signs it, under the law of the Medes and Persians, which can't be changed.
Everyone knows what Daniel does every day.

teach.b: Here is what he does: "Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime."
Look at what he doesn't do. He doesn't close the windows.
He doesn't switch to praying in secret for a month. He doesn't march into the square to make a point either. He goes home, to his own room, and does what he did yesterday.
The courage in this story looks like a habit.

teach.h: FACING A CITY HE CAN'T SEE.
teach.b: And notice which way the windows face: toward Jerusalem, a city far away. He can't see it. He faces it anyway.

teach.h: HIS WINDOWS BEING OPEN TOWARD JERUSALEM.
teach.b: The officials catch him. The king, who doesn't want this, tries until sundown to save him and can't, and Daniel goes into the den. At dawn the king runs to the stone and calls.
Daniel answers: "My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me." This chapter left marks on Jewish prayer.

Jewish tradition sets prayer for morning, afternoon and evening, said facing toward Jerusalem, and the Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, learns from this very verse that a person should pray in a room with windows.

how: Jewish tradition sets three services a day, Shacharit in the morning, Minchah in the afternoon and Maariv in the evening, facing toward Jerusalem, and the Talmud (Berakhot 31a) learns from Daniel 6 that one should pray in a room with windows.

games.q: you're Daniel. the law is signed: thirty days, no prayer to anyone but the king, or the lions. what do you do?
o: pray quietly with the windows shut until it blows over.
go home and pray as you always have, windows open.
games.why: he goes home and prays three times a day with the windows open toward Jerusalem, "as he did aforetime." no hiding, no show.

practice: If there's a window near you, turn toward it or open it a little; if not, turn toward the light in the room, and let it stand for whatever you face each day: a place, a hope, a person, God.
If you pray, this is your time, in words from your tradition or in silence, the way Daniel prayed in his own room; if you don't, simply sit facing out and let the day come in.
